Compress JPG to 20KB

JPEG is lossy, so it is the most reliable way to hit a small target. This page defaults to JPEG output at 20KB.

Compression tool

Target size Target size:
Advanced settings

By default the tool keeps quality reasonable (about 62% or higher) and reduces dimensions to reach small targets; tick “Keep dimensions” to prefer full size at lower quality. Aspect ratio is always preserved and images are never enlarged. PNG is lossless and may not reach a small target; JPEG/WebP are lossy. JPEG replaces transparency with white; WebP and PNG keep it.

Why JPG works well for small targets

The tool re-encodes your JPG at different quality levels, measures the real file size each time, and keeps the best one under 20KB.

Tips for JPG photos

Photos with smooth backgrounds compress better than detailed scenes. If the result is above target, reduce the maximum width to 300–500px.

How JPEG compression works, briefly

JPEG divides a picture into small blocks, simplifies colour and fine detail, and stores the result compactly. A quality setting controls how much detail is thrown away. Lower quality gives a smaller file but more visible blocks and blur. Because JPEG is lossy, the discarded detail cannot be recovered.

This tool encodes your JPG at different settings, measures the real output size each time, and keeps the best result under 20,480 bytes. It never assumes that a given quality number will hit a given size.

JPG, JPEG and file extensions

JPG and JPEG are the same format; the shorter extension exists because older systems limited extensions to three letters. When you download from this page, the file is a genuine JPEG and the extension is .jpg. The tool does not rename a file to look like another format.

If a form insists on ".jpeg" you can rename the downloaded file's extension without changing its contents, though most systems accept either.

Photo types and expected results

Portraits with plain backgrounds usually compress best, because large smooth areas cost very few bytes. Landscapes with foliage, crowds, and patterned clothing contain much more detail and often need smaller dimensions to fit in 20KB. Scanned documents saved as JPG may remain readable at larger widths, but small print can become fuzzy at this size.

If your result is too soft, try cropping first. A tight crop of the face or subject uses the limited bytes where they are most useful.

Avoid these mistakes

Do not enlarge a small image before compressing; it adds pixels but no detail. Do not repeatedly download and recompress the same file. Do not rely on a file extension alone when a portal checks the real format. And do not forget to keep your untouched original in case you need a different size later.

Using Advanced settings for JPG

Open Advanced settings to set a maximum width or height, adjust the minimum quality, or tick "Keep dimensions". The minimum quality value stops the tool from going below a floor you are comfortable with. If the floor stops the tool from reaching 20KB, it tells you instead of quietly producing a worse image.

Batch compressing JPGs

You can add many JPGs at once, for example a set of family photos for several application forms. Each is handled separately with its own status and its own download button. A ZIP download combines the successful files and gives each a unique name, so identically named camera files do not overwrite each other.

Fine-tuning a stubborn photo

If a JPG will not reach 20KB at an acceptable look, change one thing at a time. First crop. Then set a maximum width of around 500 pixels and run it again. If the result is still above target, try 400 or 300. Only then lower the minimum quality. Changing the width first almost always gives a cleaner picture than forcing the quality down. If you still cannot reach 20KB, consider asking whether the 50KB tool would satisfy the form.

Common questions

Does re-compressing a JPG lose more quality?

Yes. Each lossy re-encode discards some data, so keep your original file.
